rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents ignore the Prophet because they do not value his advice and reminders.
rows.anchor: if they are not listening to him, then it is because they do not value his advice and reminders.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They prefer to be caught suddenly by the Hour rather than heed the warning and prepare for the Hereafter, so the Prophet should leave them to face their heedlessness.
rows.anchor: instead of paying heed and doing some deeds for the Hereafter, they want that the hour of doom should come upon them suddenly and catch them unaware.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Day of Judgment, friends and relatives will not help; their mutual friendship will turn them into enemies because it helped bring about their eternal doom.
rows.anchor: all these friends will become mutual enemies in the Hereafter because it was this mutual friendship which became the cause of their eternal doom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By acting as yes-men instead of reflecting freely and seriously, they deprived themselves of the Prophet's and his companions' sincere counsel.
rows.anchor: If they had not been “yes-men” who support each others’ views and instead had reflected with freedom and seriousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the closest friends and relatives will be unable to benefit one another on that Day.
rows.anchor: the closest of friends and the closest of relatives will be of no benefit to a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person will grieve over what they lost and blame their friends, but their wailing will achieve nothing.
rows.anchor: every person will be dejected at his deprivation and will censure his friends. However, all these wailings be of no avail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 36–39 develop the same theme of friendship turning into enmity in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Verses 36 to 39 discuss this very issue in a very effective way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The God-fearing believers are exempt from the fate of friends becoming enemies.
rows.anchor: the believers and the pious will remain protected from this evil fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious used to counsel one another about truth and justice and to practice the counsel they gave.
rows.anchor: They used to advise and counsel one another about what was the truth and what was just and also practiced on their own counsel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because they counseled and practiced truth, the pious will rejoice in their success and greet their companions peacefully on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: they will rejoice on the Day of Judgement on their success and welcome their companions with peace and salutations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God congratulates the pious on leaving the place of trial and entering an eternal kingdom without fear or sorrow.
rows.anchor: they have entered this eternal kingdom where fear and sorrow will not bother them at all.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear concerns future dangers, while sorrow concerns past and present failures and afflictions; Paradise removes both, making the promise apt.
rows.anchor: fear relates to the dangers of the future and sorrow to the failures and afflictions of the present and the past

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in God's signs and sincere obedience are the qualities that merit this reward; a mere claim of faith without obedience does not merit it.
rows.anchor: this high status will be deserved by only those who today profess faith in His signs and follow His directives with full sincerity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word translated as rejoicing means to make someone happy and joyous.
rows.anchor: to make someone happy and joyous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azwāj can mean wives or something varied and multifarious; the author cites the varied vegetation of 20:53 as an example of the latter usage.
rows.anchor: used in the Qur’ ān to connote wives and also has some other meanings. For example, it also means something which is multifarious and has a lot of variety.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azwāj is also used for groups who share a view and accompany one another; examples are cited at 15:88, 37:22, and 56:7.
rows.anchor: On that day, you will be divided into three groups.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers reading azwāj here as groups sharing the same views and beliefs, and translates the verse accordingly.
rows.anchor: refers to groups of people holding the same views and beliefs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although believers differ in rank according to faith and deeds, all receive and fully enjoy Paradise's favors.
rows.anchor: Though the level and rank of a person will be different with respect to the extent of his faith and nature of deeds, yet all believers will be treated with the favours of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast to the disbelievers and their companions becoming enemies, believers will be happy in one another's company.
rows.anchor: Earlier, the disbelievers and their associates and friends are mentioned and it is said that they will become enemies of one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣiḥāf means plates or dishes, and the term for cups is akwāb.
rows.anchor: refers to “plates and dishes,” and the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gold is understood with both plates and cups, but its second occurrence is suppressed to avoid repetition; the translation restores the omitted word.
rows.anchor: in order to avoid repetition, it is suppressed. I have revealed this suppression in the translation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Boy-stewards will continuously serve the people of Paradise with gold plates and cups as hospitality.
rows.anchor: the boy-stewards of Paradise would continuously circulate among the companions of Paradise plates and cups of gold for their hospitality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise's food and drink will satisfy desire and delight the eyes, combining taste with attractive appearance.
rows.anchor: will not only be tasty but also eye-catching.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from indirect reference to direct address gives special attention and favor, reassuring believers that their Paradise reward is not transient.
rows.anchor: this change in style signifies special attention and favour. In other words, the Almighty will elaborately give glad tidings to them to rest assured that what they have been given is not transient in nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assurance of eternal Paradise protects its greatest delight from the disappointment of a temporary reward; believers may enjoy it without reservation, and no one can take it from them.
rows.anchor: One’s delight about the greatest of favours stands compromised if it is known that the favour is temporary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is an earned recompense and right, not merely a gift; this accords with human nature, since an unearned reward does not bring true happiness, and reflects believers' efforts for truth.
rows.anchor: instead of regarding Paradise to be a mere gift from Him, He has regarded it to be the consequence of the efforts of the inhabitants of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise will contain every kind of fruit they desire, always available without fear that the supply will diminish.
rows.anchor: there will be fruits of all kinds. Whichever they would want to eat will be at hand; there will be no fear of any reduction in this treasure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinners will remain forever in Hell's torment and will never be able to escape it.
rows.anchor: they shall always dwell in the torment of Hell; they will never be able to free themselves of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The all-encompassing torment will never be suspended, diminished, or removed.
rows.anchor: it will not be taken away from them even temporarily nor will it be reduced in extent, let alone being salvaged from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will be entirely without hope, including the far-fetched expectation of relief or release that might console someone in hardship.
rows.anchor: they will find themselves with no hope in this torment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fate is not God's injustice: He provided what was needed for guidance, but they ignored it and enslaved themselves to desire, so they wronged their own souls.
rows.anchor: Whatever arrangement was needed for their guidance was made by the Almighty; however, they did not value it; instead they spent all their lives as slaves to their desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people address Mālik, the jailer of Hell, asking him to request that God end their lives.
rows.anchor: They will ask the jailer of Hell: O Master! If there is no possibility of any mercy on us please request your Lord to finish us.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik answers that they cannot be destroyed and must remain in Hell; death, their last support in despair, is withheld from them as the greatest deprivation.
rows.anchor: The last support to despair is death, but these people will be deprived of even this support, and this indeed is their greatest deprivation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse turns again to warn Quraysh: they received the Qur'an as truth, but most reject it and should consider the fate of persisting; that fate is self-inflicted, not injustice from God.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has presented the Qur’ ān before them in the form of the truth; however, their majority is showing aversion to it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrama means to make something strong and secure; abrama al-ḥabl means to twist a rope tightly, and here the phrase means to make a final decision.
rows.anchor: Here it means to take a final decision on something.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse threatens Quraysh with decisive punishment, and changes from direct address to indirect speech to intensify the threat.
rows.anchor: to stress the threat the style has changed from direct address to indirect one
